title: Japan Earthquake Death Toll Climbs to 28 as Thousands Go Without Water in Sweltering Heat
excerpt: Two days after the 7.1-magnitude quake struck Kumamoto, rescue operations continue at a destroyed mall and paper mill while heatstroke warnings mount.
body:
• The death toll from Japan's 7.1-magnitude earthquake has risen to 28, with 17 confirmed dead in Kumamoto Prefecture and others still under investigation
  • Thousands of residents remain without running water, relying on military water bowsers limited to 3 litres per person
  • Temperatures forecast near 40°C have triggered heatstroke warnings, with Japan's Self-Defense Force installing 300 air-conditioning units in evacuation centres
  • Rescue operations continue at Aeon Mall Kumamoto and Nippon Paper Industries' Yatsushiro plant, where multiple people remain unaccounted for

A Region in Crisis

Two days after a devastating 7.1-magnitude earthquake ripped through Japan's Kumamoto Prefecture, the disaster's toll continues to mount. The death count has reached 28, according to Japan's top government spokesperson, though the Kumamoto prefectural government has confirmed 17 directly linked to the quake.

https://x.com/Reuters/status/2082100008439177556

The majority of confirmed deaths occurred at two sites: Nippon Paper Industries' paper mill in Yatsushiro, which suffered catastrophic structural damage, and Aeon Mall Kumamoto, where a possible gas explosion caused partial collapse of the second floor shortly after the quake struck at 4:27 p.m. local time on July 28.

Six people remain in cardiopulmonary arrest, and search-and-rescue teams continue to comb through rubble at both locations. Ten people are still unaccounted for at the shopping centre alone.

Water Crisis Compounds the Disaster

With water mains ruptured across the affected region, thousands of residents have been forced to queue at military distribution points. Self-Defense Force trucks have been ferrying water tanks to community centres and schools, refilling from emergency reserves beneath Yatsushiro's city hall. Each resident is limited to just 3 litres.

"It would be better if disasters did not happen, but this is Japan, so perhaps it is something we simply have to live with."

— Masahiro Miyamoto, Yatsushiro resident

Miyamoto, who had spent the day clearing rubble from a collapsed temple gate, returned home to find his own house standing beside the flattened remains of his neighbour's. The few shops still open were overwhelmed with people searching for supplies, while cars formed long queues at petrol stations, according to Reuters.

Heat Adds a Second Emergency

Temperatures forecast to approach 40°C over the weekend have introduced a dangerous secondary crisis. Kumamoto officials warned of rising heatstroke risk among the estimated 10,000 people sheltering in evacuation centres — many of them elderly.

The SDF is installing roughly 300 air-conditioning units across evacuation sites and other critical locations. Water infrastructure repair, however, has no clear timeline. "It will require painstaking work, and there is currently no timetable," a Kumamoto official told Reuters.

Scale of Destruction

The earthquake struck the central part of Kyushu island, toppling buildings, sparking fires, and damaging roads and bridges. Kumamoto airport closed its runway and cancelled flights. JR Kyushu suspended all rail services, including bullet trains. More than 100 aftershocks have rattled the region since the initial quake.

The US Geological Survey estimated that approximately 1.2 million people experienced "Very Strong to Severe" shaking, and described both landslides and liquefaction as "significant in severity and spatial extent."

What Indians in Japan Should Know

India's embassy in Tokyo has not issued specific advisories but has urged Indian nationals in affected areas to stay alert and contact the embassy's emergency helpline. Japan is home to over 56,000 Indian nationals, with significant communities in Kobe, Osaka, and other parts of western Japan within the broader quake zone. Indians travelling to or through Kyushu should check flight and rail service updates before departure.

The Bank of Japan's rate decision, scheduled for Friday, is expected to hold at 1.0%, though the earthquake's economic fallout could factor into the central bank's forward guidance.
